messages.subject_clean: placing a ggvis plot within shiny
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'll try my best to get the language right; please forgive my butchering of the vocabulary.

Using what is already functional in ggvis, I am able to do some really neat things combining with shiny - stuff that I can show off within my company and say "look at what these RStudio folks can let me do!"

Where I am banging my head right now is how to size ggvis plots so that they will conform to the shiny layout.

To my best understanding, in ggvis opts, one specifies the width and height using pixels.

In the shiny/bootstrap framework, we have panels and columns, the width of which depend on the browser's width, and may be resized.

Is there a way (or could there be a way) to specify to ggvis or to shiny to take this plot, make the width according to the width of the container, and to specify an aspect ratio to be respected in case of window resizing?

Thanks,

Ian

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I don't know if this is an issue or a user error - happy to file an issue if need be:

I am having trouble specifying the domain for datetime scales, code and session info below.

The error I get is: Error: x is not a numeric or integer vector

Related question, given a datetime scale, is it (could it be) possible to specify the timezone in which you wish to see the scale rendered? There seems to be a UTC option, but I am thinking of a case where the time is stored as "America/Pacific", but my computer is in New York. Could I see the scale rendered in Pacific time, rather than Eastern time?

I know you guys are in the middle of getting a lot of new stuff done, so I am happy to do as much legwork as you might think helpful.

Thanks,

Ian

======

library(ggvis)
library(lubridate)

# make it reproducible
set.seed(3.14)

# we will take a number of samples over the course of a day
n_sample <- 10
time_start <- ymd("2014-05-09", tz = "America/Chicago")
dur <- ddays(1)

# get our sampling times
time <- time_start + dur*runif(n_sample)

# get our observations
y <- sin(2*pi*(as.duration(time_start %--% time)/dur))

df <- data.frame(time = time, y = y)

# hardcode the domain
dom_time <- c(time_start, time_start + dur)
dom_y <- c(-1, 1)

# plot the data, specifying our hardcoded domain
ggvis(df, props(x = ~time, y = ~y)) +
  layer_point() +
  dscale("x", type = "datetime", dom = dom_time) + # this line causes error
  dscale("y", type = "numeric", dom = dom_y)

messages.subject: ggvis 0.2
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

We're very pleased to announce version 0.2 of ggvis. This represents a
major refinement of the ggvis API. The bad news is that almost
everthing has changed (if only a little), the good news is that we're
now really happy with the API and it's unlikely to have more major
changes.

The main change is that ggvis now uses a functional approach to
building plots. Instead of doing:

    ggvis(mtcars, props(~wt, ~mpg)) + layer_point()

You now do:

    layer_points(ggvis(mtcars, ~wt, ~mpg))

This is a bit clunky, but we streamline it by using the pipe operator
(`%>%`, from magrittr):

    mtcars %>%
      ggvis(~wt, ~mpg) %>%
      layer_points()

We think that this change will make it a little easier to create
plots, and just as importantly, it's made the internals of ggvis much
much simpler (so now we actually understand how it works!). As part of
these changes:

* We now have a better idea of how layers should work. These are the "magic"
  bits of ggvis - they can inspect the current state of the plot, the data and
  the visual properties and decide what to do. For an example, take a look at
  `layer_guess()` which implements the most important parts of `qvis()`,
  guessing which type of layer to use to display the data.

* `ggvis()` and all layer functions now take props directly - you no longer
  need to use `props()` in everyday work.

* You can seamlessly use data transformations from dplyr: that means that
  you use `group_by()` to define grouping in the plot, and you can use
  `filter()`, `summarise()`, `mutate()` and `arrange()` both inside and
  outside of visualisations. See `ggvis?dplyr` for more examples.

* Data transformations are now handled by `compute_*()` functions. These
  are S3 generics with methods for data frames, grouped data frames and
  ggvis objects. This means that any transformation done by ggvis for
  a visualisation (e.g. smoothing) can also be done on ordinary datasets so
  you can see exactly what variables are being created.

* It is possible to extract all the data objects, including those that are
  created by a transformation function, with the `get_data()` function. This
  makes it easier to inspect and understand what's happening to your data.

* The `explain()` function shows the structure of the ggvis object in a
  somewhat-readable format.

* New `handle_click()`, `handle_hover()`, `handle_resize()` and
  `handle_brush()` allow you to connect callbacks to important ggvis events.
  A fully reactive interface will follow in the future.

* The process of embedding ggvis plots in shiny apps has been overhauled and
  simplified. See details in `ggvis?shiny` and sample apples in `demos/apps/`.

* A new built-in dataset: cocaine, recording cocaine seizures in the US in
  2007. We plan to transition our dummy examples that use mtcars to something
  more useful/informative over time.

We've updated all the examples, demos and vignettes to help you
convert to the new syntax.  We're sorry that we had to break all your
existing ggvis code, but we're really excited about the new syntax,
and hope you will be too.

ggvis still isn't ready for CRAN (but 0.2 is a _lot_ closer than 0.1
was). It requires the latest development version of Shiny and dplyr,
so install it with:

    install_github(c("rstudio/shiny", "hadley/dplyr", "rstudio/ggvis"))

Hadley & Winston

--

messages.body_plain:
Tried that too. didn't work :(

So here's my ugly workaround:

```{r, results='asis'}
library(ggvis)
library(knitr)

plots <- lapply(1:5, function(x){
  ggvis(mtcars, ~cyl, ~mpg) %>% layer_points() %>% knit_print
})
html <- paste0(lapply(plots, unclass), collapse = "\n")
asis_output(html, ggvis_dependencies(absolute = TRUE, in_shiny = FALSE))
```

So the issue seems to be that the internal `knit_print` implementation in `ggvis` outputs a `asis` output. However, knitr couldn't understand when such output wrapped inside a for-loop. So I extracted the raw html and collapsed them into one. Glue it with ggvis dependencies for meta. That worked for me.

Not sure if we can fix this in `ggvis` or this is some work for `knitr` instead.

messages.subject: ggvis + shiny slow performance issues
messages.body_plain:
I've been working on linking plots together in ggvis + shiny using handle_click.  I've run into some performance issues and through some debugging I've found that ggvis + shiny has a slow response time for clicking when there's a large dataset loaded (~300MB).

Here's a reproducible example:

##server.r##
library(shiny)
library(ggvis)

#unused
dat <- runif(720 * 1280 * 40, 0 ,1)

select <- reactiveValues(x = 50, y = 10)

click <- function(data, ...) {
  select$x <- data[[1]]
  select$y <- data[[2]]
  print(data)
}

shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  reactive({
    mtcars %>% ggvis(~hp, ~mpg) %>%
      layer_points() %>%
      handle_click(on_click = click) %>%
      layer_points(select$x, select$y, fill := "red")
  }) %>% bind_shiny("ggvis")
})

##ui.R##
library(shiny)
library(ggvis)

shinyUI(fluidPage(
  mainPanel(
    ggvisOutput("ggvis")
  )
))

In the above example, if you click on a point in the plot it will highlight in red -- currently on my machine there is a 5-6 second delay between clicking and highlighting.  Notice above that dat <- runif(720 * 1280 * 40, 0 ,1) is a large unused dataset.  If we remove this dataset, then clicking and highlighting is basically instant.  In my original project with linked plots this larger dataset would be used for another plot that would link to the first one.

messages.subject: Re: ggvis + shiny slow performance issues
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure why you're getting the delay - the presence of dat makes no difference on my machine. Maybe you're low on memory?

At any rate, here are a few other things that might help:

It's best not to wrap the ggvis call in reactive(). I can see that you're doing it because you're referencing values from a reactiveValues object, select$x and select$y, and you can only do that within a reactive context. The problem with putting the entire ggvis call into a reactive is that each time one of those reactive values changes, the whole reactive is invalidated and a new spec needs to be generated and sent to the client. That's why you see a flash each time it updates.

A better way to do it is to add the layer_points with a reactive data source (as in data=my_reactive). ggvis knows how to handle it when the data is a reactive, and won't recompute the whole plot when you do it this way. (Note that I'm talking about reactive expressions, which are objects created by reactive(), not reactiveValues(). reactive values behave differently from reactive expressions.) For example:

library(shiny)
library(ggvis)

select <- reactiveValues(x = 50, y = 10)

select_df <- reactive({
  data.frame(x = select$x, y = select$y)

})

click <- function(data, ...) {
  select$x <- data[[1]]
  select$y <- data[[2]]
  print(data)
}

app <- list(
  server = function(input, output) {

    mtcars %>% ggvis(~hp, ~mpg) %>%
      layer_points() %>%
      handle_click(on_click = click) %>%

      layer_points(x = ~x, y = ~y, fill := "red", data = select_df) %>%
      bind_shiny("ggvis")
  },
  ui = fluidPage(

    mainPanel(
      ggvisOutput("ggvis")
    )
  )
)

runApp(app)

In the example above, you'll see the point floating around because of the update duration. You can set it to zero with set_options(duration = 0).

In the example above, the red point is on another layer. An even better way of going about it is to use just one layer of points and set the fill based on whether the item has been clicked. You'll need the latest development version of ggvis for the code below to work:

library(shiny)
library(ggvis)

select <- reactiveValues(key = NULL)

mtc <- reactive({
  selected <- rep("No", nrow(mtcars))
  selected[select$key] <- "Yes"
  dat <- cbind(mtcars, key = 1:nrow(mtcars), selected = selected)
  dat
})

click <- function(data, ...) {
  select$key <- data$key
  print(data)
}

app <- list(
  server = function(input, output) {
    mtc %>% ggvis(~hp, ~mpg) %>%

      layer_points() %>%
      handle_click(on_click = click) %>%

      layer_points(fill = ~selected, key := ~key) %>%
      scale_nominal("fill", range = c("black", "red")) %>%
      set_options(duration = 0) %>%
      bind_shiny("ggvis")
  },
  ui = fluidPage(

    mainPanel(
      ggvisOutput("ggvis")
    )
  )
)

runApp(app)

-Winston
